slides.title: Application and Web Vulnerabilities
points: Application and web vulnerabilities often look similar on the exam. The goal here is to recognize the exact failure: memory corruption, timing flaws, malicious updates, database injection, or browser-side script execution.
Security+ Objective 2.3: explain various types of vulnerabilities.

slides.title: Memory Injection
slides.teach: A vulnerability where malicious code or data is introduced into a process's memory so execution or behavior can be altered.

course.learn: A vulnerability where malicious code or data is introduced into a process's memory so execution or behavior can be altered.

breakdown.explanation: Malicious content is deliberately placed into memory.
Injected shellcode, Malicious payload placed into process memory

course.why: If an attacker can place executable content in a process's memory, they may alter program behavior or execute code.
course.example: Shellcode is injected into a running process.
course.exam: Malicious payload placed into memory → MEMORY INJECTION.
course.check_q: Which vulnerability involves placing malicious content into a process's memory?

slides.title: Buffer Overflow
slides.teach: Occurs when a program writes more data into a buffer than it can hold, overwriting adjacent memory.

course.learn: Occurs when a program writes more data into a buffer than it can hold, overwriting adjacent memory.

breakdown.explanation: Too much data is written into a space that is too small.

course.why: Overwriting adjacent memory can crash software or alter control flow.
course.example: Oversized input overwrites memory beyond a fixed-size buffer.
course.exam: Too much input for the buffer → BUFFER OVERFLOW.
course.check_q: Which vulnerability results from writing beyond a buffer boundary?

slides.title: Race Condition
slides.teach: A flaw caused by timing or ordering when multiple actions compete for the same resource.

course.learn: A flaw caused by timing or ordering when multiple actions compete for the same resource.

breakdown.explanation: The result changes depending on which operation happens first.

course.why: Attackers may exploit timing gaps to alter state after a check but before the action completes.
course.example: A file is validated, changed by an attacker, then used by the application.
course.check_q: Which vulnerability depends on timing or operation order?

slides.title: Time-of-Check (TOC)
slides.teach: The moment a system verifies a condition or permission before an action.

course.learn: The moment a system verifies a condition or permission before an action.
course.why: If the system assumes the checked state will remain unchanged, an attacker may exploit the gap.
course.example: An application checks whether a file belongs to the current user.
course.check_q: What is the moment when a system validates a condition before use?

slides.title: Time-of-Use (TOU)
slides.teach: The moment the previously checked resource is actually used.

course.learn: The moment the previously checked resource is actually used.

breakdown.explanation: The system uses the resource later.

course.why: If state changed after the check, use may occur under unsafe assumptions.
course.example: After validation, the application opens the file that has since been replaced.
course.check_q: What is the moment when the checked resource is actually used?

slides.title: Malicious Update
slides.teach: A software update that contains or delivers malicious code, often because an update mechanism or provider was compromised.

course.learn: A software update that contains or delivers malicious code, often because an update mechanism or provider was compromised.

breakdown.explanation: A trusted update is turned into a malware delivery path.

course.why: Users and systems often trust official update channels, so compromise can scale broadly.
course.example: A vendor update contains malicious code and is distributed to customers.
course.exam: Trusted update delivers malware → MALICIOUS UPDATE.
course.check_q: What vulnerability category describes malware delivered through a compromised update?

slides.title: Operating System (OS)-based
slides.teach: A vulnerability caused by weaknesses, bugs, or insecure behavior in the operating system itself.

course.learn: A vulnerability caused by weaknesses, bugs, or insecure behavior in the operating system itself.

breakdown.explanation: The flaw is in the OS layer.

course.why: OS vulnerabilities can affect every application and service relying on that platform.
course.example: An attacker exploits a kernel flaw to gain elevated privileges.
course.check_q: Which vulnerability category involves flaws in the operating system itself?

slides.title: SQL Injection (SQLi)
slides.teach: A web attack where untrusted input is interpreted as SQL commands by a backend database.

course.learn: A web attack where untrusted input is interpreted as SQL commands by a backend database.

breakdown.explanation: User input becomes part of the database query.

course.why: Unsafe query construction can let attackers read, modify, or bypass controls in a database.
course.example: A login field changes the SQL query sent to the database.
course.check_q: Which vulnerability lets user input alter SQL queries?

slides.title: Cross-site Scripting (XSS)
slides.teach: A web vulnerability where attacker-controlled script executes in another user's browser through a trusted site.

course.learn: A web vulnerability where attacker-controlled script executes in another user's browser through a trusted site.

breakdown.explanation: The attacker gets script to run in the victim's browser.

course.why: XSS can steal session data, alter pages, or perform actions in the user's browser context.
course.example: A malicious comment executes JavaScript when another user views the page.
course.exam: Script runs in victim browser → XSS.
course.check_q: Which vulnerability causes attacker-controlled script to execute in a user's browser?

blocks.title: Application vulnerability distinctions
rows: Malicious code/data is placed into process memory
Too much input overwrites buffer boundaries
System checks, state changes, then uses

blocks.title: TOC / TOU step-by-step
rows: Application verifies a file or permission.
Attacker swaps or modifies the resource.
Application uses the resource assuming the earlier check is still valid.

blocks.title: Application and web vulnerability exam shortcuts
items: Malicious payload placed into memory → MEMORY INJECTION
The defining issue is hostile code or data being introduced into memory.
Example: Shellcode is injected into a running process.
Too much input overwrites memory → BUFFER OVERFLOW
The problem is capacity: the program writes beyond the intended buffer boundary.
Example: Oversized input overwrites adjacent memory.
Check first, state changes, use later → TOC/TOU
The system validates something, but the resource changes before it is used.
Example: A file is checked, replaced by an attacker, then opened.
User input is interpreted as SQL by the backend database.
Example: A login field alters the SQL query.
Script runs in victim browser → XSS
The injected script executes in another user's browser, not directly in the database.
Example: A malicious comment executes JavaScript for visitors.
Trusted update delivers malware → MALICIOUS UPDATE
The update package or update mechanism has been compromised.
Example: Customers install a vendor update containing malicious code.
blocks.example: Memory: Memory injection = place code in memory · Buffer overflow = too much data · SQLi = database · XSS = browser.

questions.q: An application checks whether a file belongs to the current user. Before the application opens it, an attacker replaces the file with a symbolic link to a protected file. What vulnerability is this?
questions.explanation: The application checks one state, that state changes, and then the application uses the resource.

questions.q: A login field allows attacker input to alter the backend database query. Which vulnerability is this?
questions.explanation: The input becomes part of the SQL query executed by the database.

questions.q: A malicious script stored in a comment executes when another user views the page. Which vulnerability is this?
questions.explanation: The attacker-controlled script runs in the victim's browser.

questions.q: An application copies oversized input into a fixed-size buffer and overwrites adjacent memory. Which vulnerability is this?
questions.explanation: The defining issue is more data being written than the buffer can hold.

questions.q: Attackers compromise a vendor's update mechanism and distribute malware through a trusted software update. Which vulnerability is this?
questions.explanation: The malicious code is delivered through the trusted update process.

questions.q: Shellcode is deliberately placed inside a running process so the attacker can alter execution. Which vulnerability best fits?
questions.explanation: The defining behavior is malicious content being injected into process memory.

questions.q: An attacker exploits a kernel flaw to gain elevated privileges on a server. Which vulnerability category best fits?
questions.explanation: The weakness exists in the operating system kernel.
